rv.q: A sleek, smart play that lays out issues that were obvious in 1997 – and 1988 and 1959 – is welcome.

Kyoto, by Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson, is so indecently entertaining it almost feels like the result of a bet to choose the dullest, worthiest subject imaginable and make it as fun as humanly possible.
If this is infotainment, it’s infotainment deluxe.

That Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson’s play about the landmark climate change agreement is never remotely dull is a triumph against the odds to match the Protocol itself, even if its success is significantly down to co-director Stephen Daldry, who ensures that this near-three-hour marathon consistently moves with effervescent vigour.
It’s an incomparably gripping drama that will have you on the edge of your seat, complete with a script of inarguable allure and a direction that rivals its best on-screen comparisons.

Kyoto, about the behind-the-scenes battles to create the first global agreement on combating dangerous climate change, is a work of Shakespearean sweep and ambition, an invigorating and challenging piece of political theatre.
As a piece of entertainment, the production dazzles, amuses, educates and impresses.
The battle that led up to the eventual adoption of the Kyoto Protocol makes good theatre.
The growing absurdity of everyone’s behavior is, surprisingly, extraordinarily funny, best of all in the late stages.
This dramatisation of it feels “urgent” – and, go on then, I “urge” you to see it.

Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson’s blistering, darkly witty play for the RSC about the negotiations that led to the Kyoto Protocol in 1997 – the first treaty to lock down targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions – takes Pearlman as its liberal-baiting anti-hero.
Marshalling a company of 20, the directors achieve a degree of vitality that translates into urgency.
The material is extremely dull and yet it’s possible to turn dross into a gripping story if you hire a dramatist.
It’s an exhilarating evening, another slam-dunk for Nimax’s very cool new theatre.
The result is a piece of theatre that is both intellectually stimulating and timely.

cn.t: Critics hail this RSC thriller as surprisingly gripping drama wrought from dry climate negotiations, with most praising its taut storytelling and theatrical verve in making the 1997 Kyoto Protocol riveting—though one dissenter finds it dull secretarial dross.

vr.q: This is a piece of Theater which is powerful and Brilliant and important all at once.
